March 10, 1925.
Mrs. Olive B. Robinson, who has been satisfactorily serving temporarily in the
Washington General Intermediate Depot, may be appointed to a clerkship in
the War Department without reference to the civil-service rules. This action is
recommended by the Secretary of War. The Civil Service Commission does not
concur.
Done for charity.
March 10, 1925.
Mrs. Catherine Griffin may be reinstated as an operative in the Bureau of
Engraving and Printing without regard to the length of time she has been sepa￾rated from the service.
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury,
who states that Mrs. Griffin is the wife of Peter J. Griffin, who incurred disability
in the line of duty while fighting in the War with Germany and who is unable to
earn enough to support himself, his wife, and a 4-year-old child. The Civil
Service Commission concurs in recommending this order.
March 14, 1925.
Mrs. Virginia R. Guilfoyle, who served three years as yeoman (F) in the Naval
Reserve Force during the war and who was very seriously injured in an auto￾mobile accident in 1923 in which her husband, a member of an Army Reserve
Unit, was killed, leaving her with two small children dependent upon her for sup￾port, may be appointed to any clerical position under the Navy Department
which she is qualified to fill, without regard to civil service rules or regulations.
This action is recommended by the Secretary of the Navy. The Civil Service
Commission does not concur.
Done for charity.
March 16, 1925.
Mr. Albert B. Nichols may be reinstated in the classified service of the Treas￾ury Department without regard to the length of time he has been separated
from the service.
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury,
who states that it is desired to assign Mr. Nichols to the work of designing and
constructing the customs buildings in Porto Rico, for which work he is eminently
fitted by training and experience. The Civil Service Commission concurs in
recommending this order.
March 20, 1925.
Mrs. Louise M. Linthicum whose name appears on the calculating machine
operator register with a rating of 90.85 but is not within reach for certification
may be appointed in the classified service without regard to her standing on the
register. Mrs. Linthicum has been serving under temporary appointment as a
comptometer operator since June 24, 1924. The Civil Service Commission is
unable to concur in the issuance of this order.
Done for charity.
March 31, 1925.
Mrs. C. W. Salter may be appointed keeper of the Turkey Point Light Station
without reference to the provisions of the civil service rules. Mrs Salter is left
with three children without means of support by the death of her husband,
Clarence W. Salter, for many years a keeper in the Lighthouse Service. This
order is issued upon the recommendation of the Assistant Secretary of Commerce.
The Civil Service Commission submits the order without prejudice but is without
authority to recommend its issuance.
Done for charity.

April 3, 1925. 
Mrs. Anna T. Gibson may be appointed to a clerkship in the post office at
New York City without regard to the requirements of the civil service rules.
Mrs. Gibson is the widow of William A. Gibson, for 37 years a faithful employee
of the New York City post office who, at his death, left her with one dependent
child. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Postmaster General.
The Civil Service Commission is unable to concur.
Done for charity.
April 6, 1925. 
Mr. Roy A. Finney may be appointed in any department, establishment, or
office in the classified service of the United States, in any position for which his
qualifications fit him, and where there is need of his services, witliout reference
to the requirements of the civil service rules.
Mr. Finney is an honorably discharged sailor from the United States Navy,
where he served two enlistments. Following his discharge from the naval service
he was injured while employed in private industry. He passed the examination
for post-office clerk at Newark, N. J., on July 31, 1920, with an average of 80.30.
His physical condition necessitated cancellation of his eligibility.
Mr. Finney has endeavored to pass examinations for the departmental service
where physical disability is not a bar, and was a competitor in six such examina￾tions. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend this order.
Done for charity.

order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who
states that she is the daughter of a former officer in the United States Revenue
Cutter Service and a widow with a family of small children to support.

without authority to recommend its issuance.

EXECUTIVE ORDERS 121
December 1, 1925.
Mr. William A. Rogers may be reinstated as guard in the United States
penitentiary service without regard to the length of his separation from the
service.
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Attorney General and
the warden of the United States penitentiary, Atlanta, Ga., who state that,
in view of the excellent service and extended experience of Mr. Rogers, his
reinstatement would be greatly in the interest of the service.
The Civil Service Commission concurs.
December 15, 1925.
Mrs. Margaret C. Gates, a Spanish war emergency clerk, who served more
than seven years in the Post Office Department and was classified as a per￾manent clerk by the act of April 28, 1902, may be reinstated to a position with
minor clerical status in the classified civil service without regard to the time
limit on reinstatement.
Mrs. Gates is in need of employment by reason of the death, at a military
training camp, of her nephew, who was her principal support, and by the
exhaustion of his insurance.
As the Civil Service Commission can properly recommend waivers only when
the procedure under the rules will not fully meet the needs of the service,
it is unable to concur.
For charity.
December 28, 1925.
Mrs. James E. Maynard may be appointed as a skilled laborer in the Govern￾ment Printing Office without regard to the provisions of the civil-service rules.
Mr. James E. Maynard, her husband, a Spanish war veteran, after faithfu1.
and efficient service in the Government Printing Office from 1900 until Novem￾ber, 1925, was retired for total disability. He is now in a hospital and Mrs.
Maynard is in urgent need of employment for the support of herself and
11-year-old son.
Done for charity.
January 12, 1926.
Mrs. Anna M. Walsh may be appointed to a clerkship in the post office at
Boston, Mass., without regard to the requirements of the civil-service rules.
Mrs. Walsh is the wife of John J. Walsh, for 13 years a clerk in the post￾office at Boston with an excellent record for efficiency, who is totally disabled
mentally to continue his work and support his wife and three infant children.
The Postmaster General recommends this order. As the Civil Service Commis￾sion can properly recommend waivers only when the procedure under the rules
will not fully meet the needs of the service, it is unable to concur.
Done for charity.
January 19, 1926.
Mrs. Lydia F. Carroll may be permanently appointed to a classified position
in the Treasury Department without regard to the civil-service rules.
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treas￾ury who states that Mrs. Carroll has been serving in an excepted position in the
Prohibition Unit since November 3, 1923, and that her permanent appointment
as a classified employee will be in the interest of the service. She is practically
dependent upon her own labor for support, as her only son, a soldier in the
World War, has recently been retired from the Army as a first lieutenant
because of physical disability.
The Civil Service Commission is unable to concur.
Done for charity.
January 19, 1926.
Isabel L. Towner may be reinstated to the position of assistant librarian of
the National Museum without regard to the time limit on reinstatement into
the classified service.
Miss Towner was in the classified service as librarian and cataloguer from
December 1, 1909, to July 31, 1920. Since that time she has been librarian for
the National Tuberculosis Association and the National Health Council. Her
education and extensive experience with scientific publications especially
qualify her for the position in the National Museum.

February 1, 1926.
Mr. Aaron J. Stanton may be reinstated as stockman, technical stores (lum￾ber), at $7.28 per diem, in the supply department, navy yard, Pearl Harbor,

Mr. Stanton resigned without prejudice as quarterman and master boat

on May 14, 1919. No eligibles are available for appointment to this position.

order.
February 2, 1926.
Mr. Hugh S. Hanna may be reinstated in the Department of Labor as editor
in chief, $3,800 per annum, Bureau of Labor Statistics, without regard to the
length of his separation from the service.
Mr. Hanna resigned from the position of expert with a classified status,
Bureau of Labor Statistics, on March 19, 1918, since which time he has been
engaged in work similar to that required in the position to be filled and has had
constant contact with the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The Civil Service Commission recommends the reinstatement of Mr. Hanna
which is desired by the department as in the interests of the service.
February 4, 1926.
Mrs. Mabel A. Murphy may be reinstated as an operative in the Bureau of
Engraving and Printing without regard to the length of time she has been
_separated from the service.

Treasury, who states that her husband, formerly employed by the Bureau of
Engraving and Printing, has made application for retirement on account of total
disability and leaves Mrs. Murphy with two daughters to support with no
resources to speak of. She was employed in the Bureau of Engraving and

1899, to November 7, 1907.

the procedure under the rules will not fully meet the needs of the service, it is
unable to concur.
Done for charity.

Mrs. Stella Davis Mudd may be reinstated as telephone switchboard operator
in the naval powder factory at Indianhead, Md., without regard to the length of
her separation from the service.

April 17, 1926.
Capt. William T. Rigby, commissioner for the Vicksburg National Military
Park, is hereby excluded from the operation of the retirement act.
The national military parks on the battle fields of Gettysburg, Chickamauga,
Vicksburg, and Shiloh were formerly each in charge of three commissioners,
veterans of the Civil War. An act of August 24, 1912, provided that vacancies
occurring by death or resignation in the membership of the several commissions
be left unfilled.
Captain Rigby is the last surviving member of the last existing commission.
He desires to remain and the War Department desires to retain him. He is 84
years old and will have no successor.
The Civil Service Commission recommends this action.
April 23, 1926.
Mrs. Martha Fleeson may be appointed as a laborer in the post office at
Boston, Mass., without regard to the requirements of the civil-service rules.
Mrs. Fleeson is the widow of Mr. James W. Fleeson, for more than 25 years
an employee of the Boston post office, who died January 18, 1926, leaving her
with a dependent daughter, 12 years old.
As the Civil Service Commission can properly recommend waivers only when
the procedure under the rules will not fully meet the needs of the service, it is
unable to concur in the recommendation of the Postmaster General for the
issuance of this order.
For charity.
April 23, 1926.
The civil-service rule prescribing citizenship as a prerequisite for appoint￾ment may be waived in the case of Mr. Joseph Roith, in order that he may be
permitted to continue in employment as ordnance man in the Naval Gun Factory,
navy yard, Washington, D. C.
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy,
who states that Mr. Roith was born in Bavaria, Germany, on July 12, 1886,
and, when 5 years old, came to this country with his father and mother
who settled in Bloomer, Wis., and still live there; that Mr. Roith enlisted in
the United States Marine Corps on October 18, 1905, and served four years,
being honorably discharged on October 18, 1909; that he reenlisted on January
15, 1910, for four years and was appointed corporal on March 3, 1910, and
honorably discharged on January 14, 1914. He has been continuously em￾ployed at the Naval Gun Factory, navy yard, Washington, D. C., since July
9, 1914, and is now engaged in handling and loading certain pyrotechnic
materials, work for which no other employee of the Naval Establishment is
qualified, by reason of his knowledge and training. On August 22, 1924, while
Mr. Roith was engaged in handling certain pyrotechnic material, he was
severely burned and injured in a minor explosion. Mr. Roith remained out
of the military service in the late war because of the fact that his services
at the Naval Gun Factory could not be replaced without substantial material
loss to the adequate and effective operation thereof.
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in this recommendation.
April 24, 1926.
The position of special agent now held by Mr. Eugene Tyler Chamberlain
in the Department of Commerce shall be included with its occupant in the
classified service from the date of this order.
[Mr. Chamberlain was Commissioner of Navigation, by presidential appointment, from
1893 to 1921, when he was appointed special agent.]
April 26, 1926.
Mr. Harry E. Randolph may be permanently appointed in the classified serv￾ice of the Treasury Department without compliance with the provisions of
the civil-service rules.

serving temporarily in the bureau, has demonstrated his skill, and is found
to be thoroughly qualified for the work, and that his permanent appointment
is believed to be in the interests of the service.
The Civil Service Commission is unable to concur in the issuance of this
order.
Apprcved for war service.
July 17, 1926.
Mrs. Mary Graham Byrd may be reinstated in the Bureau of Engraving
and Printing, without regard to the length of time she has been separated
from the service.
This order is recommended by the Secretary of the Treasury, who states
that Mrs. Byrd served in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing from January
5, 1882, to December 18, 1918, and that on account of her previous experience
her services can be used at the present time.
As the Civil Service Commission can properly recommend waivers only
when the procedure under the rules will not fully meet the needs of the service,
it is unable to concur.
Done for charity.
July 19, 1926.
Mr. Victor Shepherd may be transferred from the position of foreman, which
is excepted from examination, to the position of clerk in the office of the
chief of quartermaster, Panama Canal Zone, without examination, under the
civil-service rules. Mr. Shepherd's transfer is recommended by the chief of
office of the Panama Canal because of his experience with the particular duties
of the position, which can be tested only with difficulty. Mr. Shepherd is
a Spanish-American War veteran and has been employed almost continuously
since 1906.
The Civil Service Commision recommends approval of this order.
August 14, 1926.
Mrs. Elizabeth Sheehan may be appointed to the position of operative in the
Bureau of Engraving and Printing without regard to the civil-service rules.
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Acting Secretary of the
Treasury, who states that Mrs. Sheehan is the widow of a veteran of the
Spanish-American War and is forced to support herself and five children.
She was employed in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing from May 1, 1920,
to April 22, 1924, without civil-service status.
The Civil Service Commission submits the case without prejudice.
Done for charity.
September 9, 1926.
Mrs. Edith P. Schaffer, an employee in the General Accounting Office, is
hereby restored to her former classified status. This order is issued upon the
recommendation of the Comptroller General, who states that by reason of her
long and efficient service Mrs. Schaffer's retention in her present position would
be advantageous. The Civil Service Commission concurs.
September 15, 1926.
Mr. Ernest H. Hubbard served as office deputy United States marshal,
Indian Territory, from July 1, 1900, to November 17, 1907, and again as chief
deputy marshal, eastern district of Oklahoma, from April 15, 1908, until June
1, 1916, the position meanwhile having been classified by order of March 2,
1909, and excepted by act of October 22, 1913.

EXECUTIVE ORDERS 127
The classified status which Mr. Hubbard retained until his separation in
1916 is hereby restored to him in his present excepted position of chief deputy
marshal. This action is taken upon the recommendation of the Acting Attorney
General. The Civil Service Commission deems the order unobjectionable.
September 20, 1926.
Thomas Rogers may be appointed to a clerical position in the Postal Service
without regard to the civil-service rules.
Mr. Rogers, a full-blooded Ankara Indian, attended for six years the Indian
State Normal Training School at Santee, Nebr. ; enlisted in a North Dakota
company; went to France; was many times cited for bravery; took an impor￾tant part in scouting, capturing at night bare-handed and alone many sentinels
who were taken back to the American camp for questioning; and was honorably
discharged July 5, 1919.
The Acting Postmaster General recommends the appointment of Mr. Rogers
under an Executive order. As the Civil Service Commission can properly rec￾ommend a waiver only when the procedure under the rules will not fully meet
the needs of the service, it is unable to concur.

NAVY-YARD SERVICE.
Adoption op Navy-Yard Regulations.
RESOLUTION OF THE COMMISSION.
Whereas the enforcement by the Secretary of the Navy of regula¬
tions governing the employment of labor at navy-yards having been
shown to be highly useful, and it being important that they should
be given stability independent of changes of Administration, and it
appearing that the examinations and other tests of fitness provided
by these regulations are based on the principles that personal fitness
should prevail over recommendation, and that political influence
should be disregarded, it is
Ordered, That these regulations be, and they are hereby, adopted as
the regulations of this Commission under the authority conferred by
clause 1 of Rule I.—Minutes of July 29, 1896, clause 4.

The regulations of the Navy Department governing the employment

All Executive orders issued from June 30, 1904, to December 30, 1905, are here
presented under the following arrangement:
(1) Orders amending the general rules and regulations.
(2) Orders amending Schedule A (classified positions excepted from examination).
Page 72.
(3) Orders affecting classifications. Page 79.
(4) Orders excepting persons named from the requirements of the rules. Page 81.
(5) Orders affecting unclassified laborers (including regulations governing the
appointment of unskilled laborers in Washington and outside of Washington).
Page 95.
(6) Miscellaneous orders. Page 101.
The Eighteenth Report, pages 161-327, contains a compilation of the civil service
rules, special orders, and classifications from May 7, 1883, to August 16, 1902. The
Nineteenth Report gives Executive orders in full for the year ending June 30, 1902,
at pages 74-92. Executive orders to June 30, 1903, appear in the Twentieth Report,
pages 65-76, and to June 30, 1904, in the Twenty-first Report, pages 76-91.
ORDERS AMENDING THE GENERAL RULES AND REGULATIONS.
ISTHMIAN CANAL SERVICE.
December 8, 1904.
The requirements as to United States citizenship may be waived for applicants for
positions on the Isthmus of Panama, under such regulations as may be provided by
the United States Civil Service Commission.
This action was taken upon the request of the Isthmian Canal Commission, because
the needs of the service could not be met without the employment of persons who
were not United States citizens.
COAST AND GEODETIC SURVEY.
February 15, 1905.
The following amendment was approved:
The requirement as to United States citizenship may be waived for applicants for
examination for the positions of officers of ships of the Coast and Geodetic Survey
on duty in the Philippine Islands under such regulations as may be provided by the
United States Civil Service Commission.
It was found by experience that citizens of the United States were not always
available to fill casual vacancies in positions on the vessels of the Coast and Geodetic
Survey, stationed in the Philippine Islands. The amendment was therefore recom¬
mended to meet these unusual conditions, with the understanding that the appoint¬
ment of aliens should be confined to cases where properly qualified Americans are
not to be had.
INDIAN SCHOOLS.
March 3, 1905.
The following Executive order was promulgated:
Section IX of Civil Service Rule II is hereby amended by adding to Section IX
the following:
A retired army officer may be appointed as superintendent of an Indian school
without competitive examination upon request of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs,
with the approval of the Secretary of the Interior, setting forth that such officer has
the required educational and business qualifications for such position, and accompa¬
nied by the authenticated military record of said officer. The Commission will then
issue the necessary certificate.

At the request of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, who declared that from
personal observation in the field he was satisfied that occasions might arise when
the proper conduct of an Indian school would require that it should have a superin¬
tendent who had enjoyed the peculiar training of an army officer, the President
promulgated the above order, amending the rules to permit such appointments with¬
out examination.
LABORERS CLASSIFIED AS CLERKS.
March 11, 1905.
The following Executive order was approved:
Laborers classified as clerks shall not receive further increase of compensation
without examination and certification under the regulation governing promotion
from the subclerical to the clerical grade.
The reasons for the promulgation of this order are set forth in the Commission’s
letter to the President on March 9, 1905, as follows:
By your order approved January 12, 1905, laborers performing classified work in
the Departments at Washington became classified laborers and subject to the same
requirements of examination for promotion as all other employees in subclerical
grades. * * *
The Commission desires to call your attention to the following facts in relation to
the laborers under consideration:
1. They entered the service without any examination or test of fitness under the
rules.
2. They acquire the status of clerks ahead of the subclerical employees appointed
upon competitive examination.
3. There is nothing in the present rules and regulations to prevent their promotion
without examination to the highest clerical positions.
The Commission is of the opinion that they should not receive further promotion
without demonstrating that they possess the requisite educational qualifications and
without compliance with the regulations which require employees to serve two years
in subclerical positions and to pass a competitive examination for promotion to clerk.
Less than this can not be required without injustice to other employees and detri¬
ment to the service.

May 1, 1905.
The requirements of three years’ service in the Philippines is hereby waived to
permit the transfer of Mr. Edward H. Hareford to the position of forest assistant in
the Department of Agriculture, in view of his services both in the Philippine and
American Forestry Services.
Mr. Hareford was for a short period a student in the American Forestry Service,
had passed the examination for forest assistant in the Philippine Service, had served
two years in that position and resigned on account of ill health. The Department of
Agriculture, in making request for the transfer, stated that Mr. Hareford’s services

May 12, 1905.
An appointment to the vacancy now existing in the position of laborer in the
Bureau of Engraving and Printing for assignment to the duties of driver of the car¬
riage of the Secretary of the Treasury may be made without examination under the
civil service rules or labor regulations.
The Secretary of the Treasury requested certification of the name of an individual

Secretary’s carriage. The individual in question, while on the list of eligibles for
this position, was not in reach for certification, but the Commission was of opinion

May 15, 1905.
Mr. John Ball Osborne may be appointed chief of the Bureau of Trade Relations
in the State Department without reference to the civil service rules.
At the request of the State Department, the Commission held an examination to
fill the vacancy existing in the position of chief of the Bureau of Trade Relations.
The employees of the Department were notified of the opportunity to be examined,
but Mr. Osborne was the only one to appear. It was discovered that Mr. Osborne

classified service. However, as he was the only one examined and his previous
record in the Government service was so satisfactory, the President was requested to
promote him by the issuance of an Executive order, which was accordingly done.
Mr. Osborne is a lawyer by profession, and was United States consul at Ghent from
1889 to 1894. In 1897 he was appointed assistant secretary of the Reciprocity Com¬

May 18, 1905.
Mr. Chauncey O. Howard may be transferred from a position of special examiner

of a criminal nature are excepted from examination. Mr. Howard was appointed to

Mrs. Relyea became a clerk in the War Department through examination in April,
1888. She was an efficient clerk and was promoted six times in a period of two years.

William J. Humphreys may be appointed professor of meteorological physics in the

After looking the whole country over, the Department has come to the conclusion

research and investigation that we wish to carry on at Mount Weather in these par¬
ticular problems. Hence it would be inadvisable and not conducive to the best
interests of the public service to open this position to competitive examination.
Professor Humphreys has been professor of physics at the University of Virginia for

ASSISTANCE TO PORTO BICAN CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION.
September 27, 1907.
The United States Civil Service Commission is directed to render such assist¬
ance as may be practicable to the Porto Rican civil service commission, created
under the insular legislative act of March 14, 1907, and officers and employees in
the Federal service in Porto Rico shall facilitate the holding of examinations
and other work of the Porto Rican civil service commission and render such
other assistance as may be practicable. The United States Civil Service Com¬
mission may, in its discretion, authorize the transfer of employees from the
civil service of Porto Rico to that of the United States, subject to the limitations
respecting transfer within the Federal civil service.
This order is similar to that signed by President McKinley on November 20,
1900, in regard to the Philippine service.
WAIVER OF EXAMINATION IN PROMOTION OR TRANSFER.
November 22, 1907.
When transfers or promotions are properly applied for and are otherwise per¬
missible, the Civil Service Commission is hereby authorized, in its discretion,
looking to the good of the public service only, to waive requirements for exam¬
ination and to substitute for such examination so waived such other tests of
fitness and capacity as the Commission may decide.
In each case where such waiver is made the reasons therefor shall be stated
at length by the Commission and made matter of record in its minutes.
This order was recommended by the Commission for the reason that it was
believed that the service would be benefited if the discretion of waiving ex¬
aminations in certain cases of transfer or promotion, where such examinations
would ordinarily be required by the rules, should be placed in the hands of the
Commission.
CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION TO AID IN EXAMINATIONS FOR DESIGNATION FOR
APPOINTMENT TO THE UNITED STATES MILITARY AND NAVAL ACADEMIES.
December 17, 1907.
Upon the request of any Member of Congress the United States Civil Service
Commission shall aid in testing the qualifications of applicants for designation
for appointment in the United States Military or Naval academies, so far as
this may be done without thereby adding to the expenses of the Commission.
As the Commission has all the facilities for holding such examinations, prac¬
tically without additional expense, it was deemed advisable to secure authority
from the President for holding such examinations.
RECOMMENDATIONS FOR LEGISLATION.
February 20, 1908.
Hereafter the following procedure shall be strictly observed by officers and
employees in the Executive civil service in submitting any recommendations
affecting the method of appointment to any position or class of positions now
included or which may be included in the classified service under the operation
of the civil-service act or rules:
Every recommendation shall be accompanied by a full statement of the rea¬
sons therefor, and, if approved by the head of the proper Department or inde¬
pendent bureau, shall be referred to the Civil Service Commission, which body
shall submit a report thereon to the President.
No recommendation of the character mentioned shall be submitted by any
officer or employee, directly or indirectly, to Congress or to any committee or
Member of Congress, except in the manner herein provided, unless such recom¬
mendation shall be called for from such officer or employee by the Senate, the
House of Representatives, or the Congress.

TWENTY-FOURTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. Ill
The purpose of this order was to prevent subordinate officials of the Depart¬
ments from attempting by subterranean methods to alter the laws, change the
powers Or duties of the Commission, or to neutralize the orders of the President
in regard to the method of appointment to any position or class of positions.
The civil-service act provides that the President shall make any necessary
exceptions from the provisions of that act requiring open competitive examina¬
tions, and any legislation which limits his discretion in that direction is in
effect a curtailment of the discretion vested in him by the act. In a number of
instances clauses have been inserted in appropriation bills excepting certain
positions from the provisions of the act and rules, at the instance or suggestion
of subordinate officials of the Department. Under this practice the Com¬
mission was given no opportunity to report to the President on any proposition
to withdraw any position from the classified service before officials in the
Department submitted to committees of Congress suggestions of such a nature.
The result of the system was that positions of a certain kind in one office
would be excepted from examination while positions of a similar nature in
another office would be subject to the provisions of the rules. Under the above
order, unless called for by Congress, no recommendation of such character
can be made without the approval of the head of the proper Department or
independent bureau, and the Civil Service Commission is given an opportunity
to report thereon.

tion if he has been appointed within less than sixty days of the establishment of
the free-delivery system therein: And provided further, That appointments in

It appears that the position demands not only a man who is capable of directing the assembling of statistical data contained in the reports of carriers subject to the law in such a manner as to make it most useful to the public and to the commission in the administration of the law, but who can also aid in directing special inquiries from time to time and is personally qualified in temperament and manner to deal with his official subordinates as well as with the officers and employees of carriers and of telegraph and telephone companies.

Mr. Edward K. Ketchum may be reinstated as a letter carrier in the Philadelphia, Pa., post office, without reference to the year limitation of the civil-service rules. This order is issued in view of injuries received by Mr. Ketchum while serving as a letter carrier and engaged in making collections of mail which resulted in serious disability, compelling him to be absent from duty frequently to such an extent that on January 14, 1904, he was compelled to resign. For this reason and in view of Mr. Ketchum’s good character, his record for faithfulness and efficiency, and the fact that he is now physically able to perform the duties of a letter carrier as testified to by the Postmaster General, and as he is not entitled to compensation under the act of May 30, 1908, granting to certain employees of the United States the right to receive from the Government compensation for injuries sustained in the course of their employ- ment, the Civil Service Commission joined with the Postmaster General in recom- mending waiver of the one-year limitation of the reinstatement rule in the interests of the service. 
January 4, 1911. 
Mrs. Florence G. Miller, widow of the late Lieut. Edward Y. Miller, United States Army, may be appointed a clerk in the classified service of the United States, subject to such tests of fitness as the Civil Service Commission may require.

130 THIRTIETH REPORT OF THE U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
August 6, 1913. 
Mr. Thomas H. Vanderford may be reinstated to an appropriate position in the Internal Revenue Service without reference to the period of his separation from the service. 
Mr. Vanderford was a deputy collector of internal revenue from October 11, 1893, to July 10, 1898, when he was removed for political reasons. A former collector of internal revenue, under whom he served and by whom he was separated from the service, makes the following statement regarding him in a letter dated May 9, 1913: “Mr. Vanderford was an officer in the service when I was appointed collector in 
1898 and had been for four years prior to my appointment. He served under me for practically a year. I regarded him as one of the best officers in the service and after 10 years’ experience as collector I think I can truthfully say he was as good an officer as I ever knew. I separated him from the service in order to appoint a man of my own party.” The Commissioner of Internal Revenue in a letter dated July 7, 1913, states that he has personally “known Mr. Vanderford for many years, that he is a man of sterling integrity, honest and fearless, and in his opinion possesses just such traits of character as would make a competent and efficient revenue officer. The records of the Internal Bevoune Bureau show that he rendered satisfactory service and was an efficient employee. 
In view of the above facts the commission concurs with the recommendation of the Sag of the Treasury and the Commissioner of Internal Revenue for the issuance of this order. 
August 9, 1913. 
Miss Sarah A. Prender, who is now serving as a skilled laborer in the Post Office Department, may be appointed to a clerical position not higher than class E on the permanent roll of that department without regard to the civil-service act. 
August 20, 1913. 
Mr. Charles M. McCabe may be reinstated as a clerk in the Postal Service without reference to the year limitation of the reinstatement rule. Mr. McCabe was removed from the Nashville, Tenn., post, office on September 10, 1898, notice of his removal alleging ‘‘inefficiency.”” No charge of inefficiency had been preferred against him and he was allowed no opportunity to reply to the charge as required by the rules then in effect. Mr. McCabe as a member of the board of civil service examiners for the Nashville post office rendered assistance to the commission in connection with investigations involving the collector of internal revenue, who was removed by the President for violation of the civil service rules. The Postmaster General states that it appears that Mr. McCabe was removed on political grounds, and the issuance of an Executive order for his reinstaterient seems to be justified by the facts in the case. In view of the facts stated above the Civil Service Commission concurs in recom- mending this order. 
August 25, 1913. 
Section 3 of the Regulations Governing Appointments to the Navy-Yard Service is hereby waived so as to permit of the appointment of Pedro Abrain to the position of 
general helper at $2.32 per diem at the navy yard, Mare Island, Cal. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy and is based upon the fact that Abrain was injured in the line of duty as a fireman on board the U. S. 8. Prometheus and is unable to perform the duties of a fireman. 
August 25, 1913. 
Section 3 of the Regulations Governing Appointments to the Navy-Yard Service is hereby waived so as to permit of the Sppeinishens of Edmond Pawellik to the position 
of general helper at $1.76 per diem at the navy yard, Norfolk, Va. This order 1s issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy and is based upon the fact that Pawellik was discharged from the Navy owing to injuries received in the line of duty and is unable to obtain civil employment. 
September 4, 1913. 
Mr. Pat O'Keefe may be appointed a deputy collector of internal revenue without examination under the civil-service rules. The commission was not consulted regarding this appointment. The reasons stated for the order are that Mr. O’ Keefe possesses excellent qualifications for work of this character, particularly in view of the income-tax provisions of the new tariff bill, and it was desirable that the collector of internal revenue for the State of Texas, where Mr. 0’ Keefe resides, should hava on his staff a man of Mr, O’ Keefe’s peculiar qualifications,

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 131 
September 11, 1913. 
Mr. James D. Scott may be reinstated in the Railway Mail Service, without regard to the length of time he has been out of the service. The Postmaster General reports that he was appointed a railway mail clerk on October 17, 1900, at $800 per annum, and promoted through the successive grades until he received a salary of $1,100 per annum; that he resigned voluntarily, April 17,1911; that his record as a clerk is good, and his reinstatement would be to the benefit of the service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending that an Executive order be issued in this case. 
September 17, 1913. 
Miss Emily W. Matter, of the District of Columbia, now temporarily employed in 
the same position through certification by the Civil Service Commission, may be appointed permanently to the position of clerk at $720 per annum in the Coast and 
Geodetic Survey. : The department in recommending this action stated that Miss Matter had demon- strated her fitness during temporary appointment, that the department had been 
unable to make selection from six certifications because of declinations and of the fact that many of the eligibles were found unsuitable. 
September 17, 1913. 
Mrs. Annie S. Renick, of the District of Columbia, may be appointed to the position of clerk at $1,000 per annum in the Department of State, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. 
September 18, 1913. 
Mr. William B. Green may be reinstated as a compositor in the Weather Bureau without reference to the time limit imposed by the civil-service rules. 
Mr. Green’s services as a compositor were terminated on December 31, 1910, after more than 20 years’ service. The reason given at the time was that a reduction of the force was necessary because of the transfer of certain work from the Weather Bureau to the Government Printing Office. The Secretary of Agriculture with the concur- rence of the Civil Service Commission recommends the reinstatement because there is reason to believe that Mr. Green was unfairly dealt with because of certain testimony he had given in a case which resulted in the reprimand of the Chief of the Weather Bureau. 
September 18, 1913. 
Mr. David A. Robbins, formerly a letter carrier at Boston, Mass., may be reinstated as a letter carrier in the Postal Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service.
